seriesStmt.p: Machine readable texts of the unpublished correspondence of James Joyce

msIdentifier.repository: Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library, Yale University

projectDesc.p: James Joyce's unpublished correspondence, collected, annotated, and made available as a digital edition

div.p: Dear Pound: I have received your card and letter dated feria sexta in Parasceve and am glad to hear that the first part of the Telemachia has appeared in your review. I shall consider it a great favour if you will kindly send a copy of this and subsequent numbers to the following addresses:

list.item: Mrs Murray , 10 Fairfield Road, Church Road, Dublin.
Messrs Slack, Monro, Saw and Co , solicitors, 70 Queen Street, London, E.C.

div.p: since it seems that the appearance of the book in The Egoist will be delayed. I request you to charge the amount against the balance of serial rights coming to me. I should also be glad to receive through you as quickly as possible a copy of each number of the review as mails from New York are somewhat uncertain.

I shall send you tomorrow the second episode of the odyssey, the lotophagoi. I am sorry you do not like the Calypso-Penelope episode. The text however is to remain exactly as I wrote it. As regards the Greek or other translations of my book I fear that the probability is rather remote. Of course I should feel highly honoured by such a translation not merely because it would bring my poor writings to the lands of many good friends of mine but also because the spirit which has sustained me so long in my labour has been that of a great Greek poet.
I have suggested to Miss Weaver that her journal be printed in Paris and Messrs Georges Crès et Cie have been so kind as to offer to place their printers at her disposal.
I regret to hear of Mr Quinn’s illness and beg you to convey my wishes for his recovery. May I ask you also to transmit to Miss Anderson my thanks for her courage and enterprise.

I do not know whether my play Exiles has been published in London or New York or whether it has been given or will be given by the Stage Society of London or whether Yeats has now reorganized his theatre in such a way as to make a production of it possible. If you know anything about it I shall be glad to hear when you write next.

I assume that you are now quite recovered. I am also well enough but suffer occasionally. The climate is, as always, very unfavourable. Life also is extremely dear. For instance coal was £14 a ton here during the winter (which is not yet over) and the prices of all things go up and up. I shall look forward to a renewal of the treasury grant made me two years ago and need scarcely say that if it be doubled I shall be doubly grateful. In view of all circumstances of the case it might be well be for the purchasing value of money has fallen by more than fifty per cent. You are not to understand this as addressed in any way to yourself as editor. You have done everything possible and I am more than repaid for my contributions. Miss Weaver, I fear, has made a very bad affair and I shall try, if she does not find a printer for her journal in Paris, to secure for her at least the English book rights so that the serial fees paid me may count as an advance of royalties.

div.note: After returning to Zurich in January 1918 from their stay in Locarno, Switzerland, JJ and family moved into a flat at Universitätstrasse 38, remaining there until October 1918, when they moved to Universitätstrasse 29.
Latin for “the sixth day of the Preparation,” the liturgical name for Good Friday. JJ refers to Pound’s letter dated “Good Friday [29 March] 1918. 12:07 a.m.” (Pound/Joyce 131).

In Locarno, JJ had finished the first three episodes of Ulysses – “Telemachus,” “Nestor,” and “Proteus” – and sent them off to Zurich to be typed, thence to be transmitted to Pound for serialization in the New York magazine The Little Review, of which Pound was foreign editor. JJ referred to these episodes collectively as the “Telemachia,” part one of Ulysses. “Telemachus” was printed in the March 1918 number of The Little Review.

Josephine Giltrap Murray (1862-1924) was JJ’s aunt, with whom he remained close all her life and on whom he depended for advice about practical matters and for detailed information about Dublin that helped him with his writing, especially Ulysses. Josephine stepped into a maternal role for JJ and his siblings after the death of their mother in August 1903, and she took a genuine interest in JJ’s aspirations to being an author. She appears briefly as Stephen Dedalus’s Aunt Josephine, wife of Richie Goulding, in chapter two of A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man, and is in Stephen’s thoughts about the Goulding family in the “Proteus” episode of Ulysses.

London solicitors who had informed JJ in February 1917 that an anonymous “admirer of [his] writing” had gifted him £200, to be paid in £50 installments in May, August, and November 1917 and February 1918 (LII 389). JJ thought that Pound was involved, but the admirer was later revealed to be Harriet Shaw Weaver (1876-1961).

Pound had written JJ on 29 March 1918 of the efforts to serialize Ulysses in the London magazine The Egoist: “The Egoist printers wont set up the stuff at all” (Pound/Joyce 131). Only a few episodes of Ulysses – “Nestor,” “Proteus,” “Hades,” and part of “Wandering Rocks” – appeared in The Egoist in 1919, because the editor, Harriet Shaw Weaver (1876-1961), had difficulty in finding a printer who would risk producing even these relatively tame portions of the book (Ellmann, JJ 443).

“Lotus-Eaters” is the second episode of what JJ called the “Odyssey,” chapter two of Ulysses, and the fifth episode of the book as a whole. In this episode, Leopold Bloom visits the post office to retrieve a letter from his erotic correspondent, Martha Clifford, observes a Roman Catholic mass in progress, looks in at a chemist’s shop about a lotion for his wife Molly, and imagines himself soaking luxuriously in a tub at the public baths – all events that connect with themes of drowsy pleasure and narcotic forgetfulness. In Book 9 of The Odyssey, Odysseus tells of his visit to the land of the lotus-eaters – or lotophagoi – who give some of his men the lotus flower to eat, rendering them forgetful and indifferent to returning home, and causing Odysseus to force them back to the ships to resume the journey for Ithaca. “Lotus-Eaters” appeared in The Little Review, vol. 5, no. 3 (July 1918): 37-49.

Pound had received JJ’s typescript of “Calypso,” the fifth episode of Ulysses, and wrote JJ on 29 March 1918 that, while the episode contained “excellent things,” he felt that the scene in which Leopold Bloom defecates, the use of the word “urine,” and other elements were simply “bad writing” and “stronger [language] than you need” (Pound/Joyce 131). He urged JJ to “[l]eave the stool” to musical hall comedians, and worried that the episode as written might lead to suppression of The Little Review, John Quinn’s withdrawal of funds for paying contributors, and the jailing of “our august editress,” Margaret Anderson (Pound/Joyce 131). Despite JJ’s insistence here that nothing be altered in “Calypso,” Pound did expurgate certain passages for serial publication (Paul Vanderham, “Ezra Pound’s Censorship of Ulysses,” James Joyce Quarterly, vol. 32, nos. 3-4 [Spring-Summer 1995]: 583-95). He told John Quinn that he had “deleted about twenty lines before sending it off to N.Y.” (Pound/Joyce 132). Thus altered, “Calypso” appeared in The Little Review, vol. 5, no. 2 (June 1918): 39-52.
JJ’s phrase, “the Calypso-Penelope episode,” may suggest that Molly Bloom combines in this episode the Homeric roles of Odysseus’s wife Penelope and the nymph Calypso, who, as related in Books 5 and 7 of The Odyssey, kept Odysseus as a forced bedmate for seven years on her island, Ogygia. Joyce scholars have argued for this merger of roles, perhaps in association with “The Bath of the Nymph,” a color print that hangs over the Blooms’ bed (U 4.369-73; see, e.g., Hugh Kenner, Ulysses [Baltimore, MD: The Johns Hopkins University Press, 1980], 27-28).

Hinting that he planned to excise certain objectionable passages from “Calypso,” Pound facetiously consoled JJ in his 29 March 1918 letter: “Perhaps an unexpurgated text of you can be printed in a greek or bulgarian translation later” (Pound/Joyce 131).

Because English printers refused to produce numbers of The Egoist containing installments of Ulysses, JJ suggested to the magazine’s editor, Harriet Shaw Weaver, that she have the printing done in Paris by less squeamish artisans, but she did not do so (LI 112, 113). Georges-Célestin Crès (1875-1935) was a publisher and bookseller who founded Crès et Cie in Paris in 1913, and in 1916, urged by the French Minister of Foreign Affairs, opened a French bookstore in Zurich, Les Éditions Françaises. In October 1917, that bookstore agreed to take seven copies of a new English edition of A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man, to be published in March 1918 by the Egoist Ltd. in London. JJ also hoped that Crès would publish a French translation of the novel, but this did not happen (LII 408). However, the Paris house, Éditions de La Sirène, which published the French translation of A Portrait by Ludmila Savitzky (1881-1957) in 1924, was managed during financial difficulties by Éditions Crès, beginning in 1923.

Pound told JJ in his 29 March 1918 letter that the New York lawyer and patron of the arts, John Quinn, “has been in hospital for a major operation” (Pound/Joyce 131). Quinn had had surgery “to remove a bleeding ulcer from which he took months to recover” (The Selected Letters of Ezra Pound to John Quinn, 1915-1924, ed. Timothy Materer [Durham, NC: Duke University Press, 1991], 137).

Pound warned JJ in his 29 March 1918 letter that The Little Review, founded and coedited by Margaret Caroline Anderson (1886-1973, might be suppressed if it published anything regarded as legally obscene in the Ulysses installments, adding, “AND I cant have our august editress jailed, NOT at any rate for a passage [the scene of Leopold Bloom defecating] which I do not think written with utter maestria [mastery]” (Pound/Joyce 131).
Exiles was published simultaneously by Grant Richards in London and B.W. Huebsch in New York in May 1918.

Despite the efforts of JJ and others, the London-based Incorporated Stage Society did not produce Exiles at this time (see JJ to Pound, 5 June 1917, notes). The Society finally presented the play at London’s Regent Theatre on 14 and 15 February 1926, with W.G. Fay as director.

On 26 August 1917, W.B. Yeats (1865-1939) explained to JJ that Exiles was “a type of work [that the Dublin Abbey Theatre] have never played well” since it was “too far from the folk drama.” In addition, the Abbey had lost some of its players as a result of a dispute and for other reasons. But essentially Yeats thought Exiles “[not] at all so good” as A Portrait (LII 405).

It is unclear what Pound had recovered from. Three months later, on 17 July 1918, he would write that he was “flat on my back with some crotchety variant of the chill-cum-flu-cum-spew” (Pound/Joyce 144).

JJ suffered a severe attack of glaucoma in Zurich in August 1917. Once he had sufficiently recovered from eye surgery, he went with his family to Locarno in October 1917 and stayed there until January 1918, partly to recuperate further.
In August 1916, with help from Pound, W.B. Yeats, and others, JJ had obtained a grant of £100 from the British Civil List (Ellmann, JJ 406).
In a letter to Nora Barnacle dated 10 September 1917, Pound mentioned that he hoped to pay JJ £50 or more, in due course, for the serialization of Ulysses in The Little Review (Pound/Joyce 125-26).

On 8 March 1918, Harriet Shaw Weaver (1876-1961), editor of The Egoist in London, sent JJ £25 as “the second payment from the Egoist for the serial rights of your novel Ulysses” (The Cornell Joyce Collection: A Catalogue, ed. Robert E. Scholes [Ithaca: Cornell University Press, 1961], 199-200). In a letter of 18 May 1918 to Weaver, JJ proposed “to cede … the book rights [to Ulysses] and to consider the sums already advanced by you for serial rights as an advance of royalties to be written off, if you agree, in two or three deductions from sums eventually due to me by half yearly accounts of sales” (LI 113). The first English edition of Ulysses was published in October 1922 “for [Weaver’s] Egoist Press, London[,] by John Rodker, Paris[,] 1922” (John J. Slocum and Herbert Cahoon, A Bibliography of James Joyce [New Haven: Yale University Press, 1953], 26).
